extracted.intended_audience: clinicians and other healthcare professionals who act as peer reviewers for The BMJ
extracted.subtask_description: Official guidance for reviewers asked to assess manuscripts for The BMJ, covering open peer review, confidentiality, competing interest disclosure, practical steps for accepting/declining, and detailed appraisal criteria for all and for research articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review and signed reports
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ has fully open peer review for all articles that undergo review. Reviewers are asked to sign their reports and agree to have their signed comments posted if a paper is published. Accepted research and analysis papers will usually have their prepublication history posted (previous manuscript versions, study protocol, committee report, reviewers’ comments, and authors’ responses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepublication history is normally posted around the time the paper is published; there may be delays. For rejected research papers, authors must keep the identity and comments of peer reviewers confidential (authors may share peer review comments—but not reviewer names—with other journals in confidence). Open peer review does not allow authors to contact reviewers directly; all queries should go through the editorial office. As a reviewer you will be advising the editors who make the final decision. Because reports may be published with your name, do not make comments you are not prepared to stand by publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of unpublished manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Unpublished manuscripts are confidential and must not be disclosed to anyone except a professional colleague whose input you request as part of your review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you discuss the manuscript with a professional colleague you are responsible for ensuring they are fully aware of the confidential nature of the discussion and that they must not disclose any information about the manuscript until the article is published. You must not disclose any information about an unpublished manuscript, including your review of it. You may refer to The BMJ and the fact that you have reviewed an article for it, but you may not post any details of the article which was reviewed, or any part of the review that would breach confidentiality. If you want to pass the manuscript to someone else to review or suggest alternatives email papersadmin@bmj.com first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare competing financial interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are asked to sign their reports and declare any competing interests on any manuscripts they review. A competing interest exists when professional judgment concerning a primary interest may be influenced by a secondary interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The BMJ restricts its direct questions to competing financial interests. Please answer whether in the past five years you have: accepted reimbursement for attending a symposium; received a fee for speaking; received a fee for organising education; received funds for research; received funds for a member of staff; received fees for consulting; been employed by an organisation that may gain or lose financially from publication; held stocks or shares in such an organisation; acted as an expert witness on the subject; or have any other competing financial interests (specify). The guidance also asks you to consider disclosing other non‑financial interests that would embarrass you if they became known (examples: close personal relationships, academic rivalry, political membership, deep convictions). The editors are not aiming to eradicate competing interests but want to be informed; a competing interest will not automatically lead to rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and appropriateness to accept a review
rubrics_metrics.description: Agree to review only if you are able to return a review within the proposed or mutually agreed time-frame and you feel qualified to appraise the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot review, it is helpful to make suggestions for alternative reviewers based on their expertise and without any influence of personal considerations or any intention of the manuscript receiving a specific outcome. If you would like to pass it on to someone else to review or suggest alternatives please email papersadmin@bmj.com first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide detailed, constructive comments with references
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should give detailed and constructive comments (with references, whenever possible) that will both help editors make a decision and help authors improve the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments may be posted with your name if the paper is published, so ensure they are professional and that you are willing to stand by them publicly. Use references to support claims about originality, omissions, or methodological concerns. Provide actionable suggestions when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: General appraisal: importance, relevance, novelty, clarity (for all articles)
rubrics_metrics.description: For all article types consider: Is the article important? Will it help readers make better decisions and, if so, how? Will the article add enough to existing knowledge? Does the article read well and make sense? Does it have a clear message?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use discretion for non‑research articles; some article types need more specific appraisal. It may be helpful to consult resources for authors, advice on article types, and the journal's transparency policy. Tailor comments to how the article will help the BMJ's mainly doctor readership to make decisions about practice, policy, education, or research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality (research articles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality — does the work add enough to what is already in the published literature? If so, what does it add?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Please cite relevant references to support your comments on originality and identify any prior work that has been overlooked. Consider whether a general medical journal is the right place for the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance to general readers (research articles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Importance of the work to general readers — does this work matter to clinicians, researchers, policymakers, educators, or patients? Will it help readers to make better decisions and, if so, how? Is a general medical journal the right place for it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment on the breadth and applicability of the findings beyond the study setting and population, and whether the results would influence clinical practice, policy, or future research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific reliability (research articles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the scientific reliability of the study: research question, overall design, participants, and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the research question is clearly defined and appropriately answered; whether the overall study design is appropriate and adequate to answer the question; whether participants are adequately described (conditions defined, inclusion/exclusion criteria described) and representative of patients affected by the evidence; and whether methods are adequately described with a clear main outcome measure. Check that the study is fully reported in line with the appropriate reporting statement/checklist (see EQUATOR Network) and consider whether the study was ethical (which may go beyond simply whether it was approved by an ethics committee or IRB).

rubrics_metrics.name: Results (research articles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the results answer the research question? Are they credible and well presented?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the completeness and clarity of results, appropriateness of analyses, presentation (tables/figures), handling of missing data, and whether reported effect sizes and uncertainty measures are adequate and interpretable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation and conclusions (research articles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the interpretation and conclusions warranted by and sufficiently derived from/focused on the data? Are they discussed in the light of previous evidence? Is the message clear?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for overinterpretation, unwarranted causal claims, failure to acknowledge limitations, and whether alternative explanations are adequately considered. Check consistency between results, abstract, and conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: References: currency and relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the references up to date and relevant? Are there any glaring omissions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify missing key citations, seminal prior studies, or recent evidence that might change interpretation. Suggest pertinent literature where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract/summary/key messages accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the abstract/summary/key messages reflect accurately what the paper says?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure numerical results and conclusions in the abstract match the manuscript. Check that key messages do not overstate findings and that they are useful for the BMJ readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental documents and reporting checklists
rubrics_metrics.description: Do documents in the supplemental files (e.g., checklists for reporting statements such as CONSORT, PRISMA, STROBE, and the trial protocol) properly match what is in the manuscript?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether supplemental documents contain information that should be reported in the manuscript or raise questions about completeness/consistency. Use the EQUATOR network resources to identify appropriate reporting standards and their extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggest alternative reviewers ethically
rubrics_metrics.description: If you decline to review, suggest alternative reviewers based on expertise and without personal influence or intent regarding the manuscript outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide names and contact details where possible, avoid nominating close collaborators or those with obvious conflicts, and ensure suggestions are based on objective expertise rather than personal preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co‑reviewing: disclose co‑reviewer identity and their competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: If you involve a colleague in the review (co‑reviewer), the identity of any co‑reviewer and any potential conflicting or competing interests they may have must be disclosed when submitting your review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure any colleague consulted is fully aware of confidentiality requirements. If you want them to take over or formally review, contact papersadmin@bmj.com first and disclose their details and potential conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reporting statements and checklists (EQUATOR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should check that studies are fully reported in line with appropriate reporting statements/checklists (collected at the EQUATOR Network).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to relevant checklists (CONSORT, PRISMA, STROBE, etc.) and confirm whether key checklist items are present in the manuscript and consistent with any submitted checklists or protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report ethics concerns, plagiarism, duplicate publication, or fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are concerned about ethics aspects of a manuscript or suspect plagiarism, duplicate publication, or scientific fraud and misconduct, refer to The BMJ's transparency policy and notify the editorial office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the journal's editorial/transparency policies for guidance on handling suspected misconduct and provide evidence or specific concerns to editors rather than making public accusations. The BMJ provides pages with advice on what to do in these situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article provenance statement
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ will add a provenance statement to accepted articles indicating who had the idea for the article and whether it was externally peer reviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible provenance options include: Not commissioned; externally peer reviewed; Not commissioned; not externally peer reviewed; Commissioned; externally peer reviewed; Commissioned; not externally peer reviewed; Commissioned, based on an idea from the author; externally peer reviewed; Commissioned, based on an idea from the author; not externally peer reviewed. Reviewers should be aware their review may be referenced in provenance information when relevant.
